desc:
Each element [l, r] of intervals stands for the set of all integers from l to r inclusive. Put all those integers into one big set S.

Return the number of blocks of S: a block is a maximal run of consecutive integers x, x+1, ..., y that all belong to S (with x - 1 and y + 1 not in S). Note that intervals which do not overlap but sit directly next to each other, like [1, 2] and [3, 4], form one block because 2 and 3 are consecutive integers.

intervals = [[7, 9], [1, 2], [3, 4], [20, 20]]
result    = 3

The blocks are 1..4, 7..9 and 20..20.
hints: Listing all integers works only for tiny ranges. Think about how to decide, from the endpoints alone, whether two intervals belong to the same block.
Sort by l. A new block starts exactly when the next interval begins after the current right-most covered integer, with a gap of at least one missing integer in between.
Track reach, the largest r seen so far. If l > reach + 1, a new block starts (count it); in any case set reach = max(reach, r).
editorial: Compared with ordinary interval merging, the only difference is what counts as 'connected'. Integer intervals [a, b] and [c, d] with b + 1 = c leave no integer uncovered between them, so they belong to the same block. That is why the test is l > reach + 1 instead of l > reach.
Sort the intervals by left end and sweep once while keeping the furthest right end. Each time the gap condition holds, a new block begins. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.
